corrosive

/kuh-ROH-siv/ — stress on ROH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something corrosive slowly eats away at or destroys whatever it touches, whether that is metal, tissue, or something more abstract like trust.

Road salt is corrosive, which is why winter cars rust from the bottom up.

Example

The constant criticism had a corrosive effect on his confidence; by semester's end, he barely believed in his own abilities.

Corrode (eat away) + -ive (having the quality of): the criticism has the quality of gradually eating away at his confidence. More precise than 'damaging' because corrosive emphasizes the slow, gradual wearing-away rather than sudden harm.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

destructive: Destructive covers any serious damage, however it happens — a flood, a crash, or a fire can all be destructive in one violent moment. Corrosive is narrower: the damage arrives gradually, as the thing is eaten away bit by bit over time.

erosive: Erosive describes gradual wearing-away by natural forces, the way wind grinds down rock or a river carves its bank. Corrosive damage is also slow, but it eats into a thing chemically or from within — the way rust spreads, or mistrust hollows out a friendship.

abrasive: Abrasive things wear a surface down by scraping and friction, like sandpaper — and an abrasive person grates on others the same way. Corrosive damage needs no rubbing: it eats into whatever it touches and keeps deepening on its own long after the first contact.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

constructive: helping to build or improve

restorative: helping repair or bring back health

Where it sits · how steadily the damage deepens

irritating → harsh → caustic → corrosive

irritating vs. corrosive: An irritating remark stings for a moment; a corrosive one keeps eating away at a friendship.

harsh vs. corrosive: 'Harsh' hurts on contact, but corrosive damage deepens steadily over time.

caustic vs. corrosive: A caustic comment burns sharply, while corrosive is the strongest — it slowly destroys whatever it touches.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — corros-: shifted stem of corrode — from Latin corrodere, 'to gnaw away' (root rodere, 'to gnaw') (Latin)

Suffix — -ive: having the quality or tendency of (Latin)

Put it together: Corrode swaps its -de ending for -s- before -ive: having the quality of gnawing away — slowly destroying whatever it touches, whether metal or a friendship.

Use the root in a new word: corrosion: Mechanics check the battery terminals for corrosion at every oil change.

Word Choice

formal

Reach for corrosive when something gradually destroys or wears away, whether it's a physical substance (like acid on metal) or something abstract (like mistrust in a relationship). The key is the slow, incremental damage.
